title: A shaded square
bodyMd:
A fictional town planted young trees in a public square after residents complained of summer heat. In the first year, a survey found little change in afternoon surface temperatures. A newspaper called the project a failure. The landscape team replied that the young crowns covered only a small area and that the proposal had forecast substantial shade only after several years. It also noted that watering and soil conditions would affect whether the trees reached that size.

The team did not ask to be exempt from evaluation. It proposed measuring survival, crown growth and actual shade each year, then comparing results with the original timetable. A delay built into a proposal should not be confused with an excuse invented afterward; equally, a long timetable should not shield a project from signs that it is off course. The useful question was whether the observed development matched the stated path toward the intended benefit.
